steps.caption: White to move. Several queen checks are possible. Some end the game on the spot and some give the king a square. Before you go on, pick one you think is mate.

steps.prompt: Which check would you play, and what do you expect the black king to be able to do after it?

fields.label: My check, and what the king can do:

steps.text: **The question.** A queen can check a king in many ways, but only some checks end the game. By the end of this lesson you will test any queen check with three short questions, find a supported check in one move or two, and explain to a friend why one check mates at once while a near twin only draws or takes longer. Marks: [V] verified here, [I] inference, [H] a guess worth testing.

steps.caption: A mating check. The queen on h5 would also mate; the other checks give the king a square.

line.say: The queen checks along the h-file from far away. Her king covers g8 and g7, and the file covers h7. Nothing is left: checkmate.

steps.caption: The near twin: another check, one move slower.

line.say: This check looks just as forcing, and the queen eyes the corner. But it leaves a square.
Black has exactly one reply: the king steps to h7, the one square this check did not cover.
Now the queen lands beside the king on a square the white king protects: mate. The twin is slower, not wrong. It leaves one flight square, so mate takes two moves.

steps.caption: Black king g8, white king g6. The queen can check from far away or from right beside the king.

line.say: The queen lands beside the king, protected by the white king. Between them they cover every neighbouring square.

steps.caption: The kings face each other with one square between them. Nothing needs protecting, because the black king can never reach the queen.

line.say: A check from the far corner. The white king covers the three squares in front of the black king; the queen covers the rest of the rank.

steps.caption: Black to move. The colours are reversed, and now two different mates exist: one beside the king, one on the h-file.

line.say: Black's queen lands beside the white king, protected by the black king. White has no square and cannot take her.

steps.caption: In a corner the king has only three neighbours, so there is less to count.

line.say: The queen takes the middle neighbour, protected by the king on b3. The king on a1 has nowhere to go.

steps.caption: White to move: mate in two. The queen cuts the king off, then the white king protects the final check.

line.say: The queen covers the whole seventh rank. The black king has one square left.
Black's only legal move is the king to g8.
Check. The white king on f6 protects the queen, so the king cannot take her. Checkmate.

steps.caption: The queen sits on the seventh rank, but her own king stands in the way. One king move can fix two things at once.

line.say: The king steps off the rank. That opens the queen's line to h7, and the king now covers g7.
Black's king goes to g8.
The queen goes beside the king on a square the white king protects. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Black's king is boxed in the corner. White's king is two steps away, and the queen is already far off.

line.say: The king steps up to the second rank, where it covers b1, b2 and b3.
The black king goes to a2, its only free square.
The queen checks along the a-file from far away. The king on c2 covers the squares beside the black king. Checkmate.

steps.text: **Count the squares.** A mate must settle the king's own square (the check) and every neighbour it could step to: up to eight, fewer at an edge. Edward Lasker (*Chess Strategy*, lectures 7 and 8) frames mating as counting squares, with the checking piece safe (checked in our notes). [V] All 364 mating positions of king and queen against a bare king, enumerated here, have the lone king on the edge. [I] In the middle, one queen and one king cannot cover eight neighbours and stay safe.
steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

steps.text: **Three questions for any queen check.** 1. Can the king take her? 2. Is any neighbouring square free? 3. If it is not check at all, does Black still have a legal move? Ask them in this order before every queen move, and the draw traps disappear. Driving the king to the edge is the next skill: see the lesson 'King and queen against king: shrink the box'.

steps.caption: Black to move and checkmated. The five squares around the king are marked. The queen and the white king between them cover all five; f7 and h7 are covered twice.
The same black king, but the white king stands on e6, two files away from the corner squares.

line.say: A check along the back rank, but the king on e6 is too far away to cover g7 or h7.
The king simply steps off the rank. A check is not yet a mate.

steps.caption: Same position again. This check looks more forceful, because the queen goes right beside the king.

line.say: The queen lands beside the king, and nothing protects her.
The king takes the queen. Only two bare kings remain: a draw.

steps.caption: Same position, third try. Quiet king moves also keep the win; one of the neatest is the king step to f6.

line.say: The patient move: the king steps nearer, so that it covers g7 and the squares beside it.
Suppose Black steps into the corner.

Now the queen lands beside the king on a protected square: checkmate. If Black goes to f8 instead, the queen's check on the back rank is mate, because the king on f6 covers e7, f7 and g7. [V: search here] This mates in two; several other quiet moves win more slowly.

steps.text: **Who needs protection?** A king can capture only on a square beside it. So a check from far away needs no protector; it needs every flight square covered. A check from beside the king must be protected, or the king takes the queen. [I] 'Protect the queen' is a good slogan up close and a poor one at long range: ask *can the king take her, and where else can it go?*

steps.caption: A king in the middle has up to eight neighbours, and here five legal replies, so no single check can mate it. Mate happens at the edge, so the king must first be driven there. [V]
Black to move, not in check, with no legal move. This position came from the kings-facing position, one queen move away from mate.

steps.text: **The stalemate trap.** The last queen move can leave the lone king with no legal move and no check: a draw, not a win. [H] It happens when attention jumps from the king's squares to the squares the queen covers, so the 'tighter' move feels better. Ask: does it give check? If so, can the king take her and is any square free? If not, does Black still have a legal move?

**The quiet move.** Often the queen cannot give mate yet, so you first take away the king's last squares. A quiet move works when every reply loses. Count Black's legal moves after yours: when one is left, the mate usually shows. The king helps by covering squares, and by standing ready to protect the queen. [H] Learners may like the close check because it feels nearer the kill; it also needs a protector.

steps.caption: Black's king on d8 has several squares. No check is mate yet.

line.say: A quiet move: the queen covers the whole c-file and checks nothing.
The king goes to e8, its only free square.
The queen checks along the back rank, with the kings facing each other. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Here a king move comes first. Whatever Black replies, a queen check follows on the first rank.

line.say: The king covers a2, b2 and c2, so the black king cannot come up the board.
Black chooses a1. The other choice, c1, also loses to a queen move.
The queen checks along the first rank. The king on b3 covers the second rank. Checkmate.

steps.caption: The king steps in front of the black king and the queen waits on the side. One careless queen move later would be stalemate.

line.say: The king steps up, covering g7 and h7. Only g8 is left for the black king.
The king goes to g8.
The queen checks along the back rank. The king on g6 covers f7, g7 and h7. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Sometimes the first move is itself a check that forces the king to one square.

line.say: A check that covers g8 and g7. Only h7 is left for the king.
The king goes to h7.
The queen lands beside the king, protected by the white king. Checkmate.

fields.label: The small change, and what it did:

steps.text: **Two real endings.** These come from rated online games played in January 2013, in the free Lichess database (CC0). The side with the queen was rated about 1450 in the first and 1340 in the second [V] from the game record. Moves are facts, the comments are ours. In each ending, ask the three questions before you read the comment.

steps.caption: Lichess game 8fn548ue. Black to move, in check on the h-file.

line.say: Black's king was in check on the h-file and stepped to g1.
White's king steps to f3. From there it covers e2, f2 and g2.
Black's king goes to f1.
The queen checks from the corner along the first rank, and the king on f3 covers the squares in front of the black king. Checkmate.

steps.caption: Lichess game 7jgv1v62. The lone king is in check and has a single legal move.

line.say: White's king was in check from the queen, and this was its only legal move.
The queen lands beside the king, protected by the black king on f6. Checkmate.

steps.text: **Recap.** Three questions for any queen check: can the king take her, is a neighbouring square free, does Black still have a legal move? A check beside the king needs a protector. From far away, the king and the edge must cover the flight squares. Quiet moves prepare it. No check and no move is a draw. Your task: explain this to a beginner, in your own words, with a position they could set up.

steps.prompt: Teach it back to an imagined beginner. Then check your answer: did you say when it works, when it fails, give a position a beginner could set up on a board, and name one mistake?
